sources.lead: Every calculation cites public literature; the methods and their names belong to their authors. Among them:
sources.list: Banister's training-response model, Tobler's hiking function, the metabolic cost of pack weight, Riegel's distance conversion, Palladino's running power, Joe Friel's heart-rate zones, Uphill Athlete's AeT (aerobic threshold) test, Jack Daniels' return after a break, and the international consensus on heat acclimation.

faq.watch.q: Which watch do I need? Can I use it without COROS or Garmin?
faq.watch.a: Yes. FIT files from any watch can be imported, and intervals.icu can be connected.
faq.power.q: No power meter — can I use it?
faq.power.a: Yes. With the power meter set to none everything runs on heart rate and pace: easy and long runs by heart rate, flat intervals and tempo runs by pace, the calculator on a heart-rate model; power charts, power options and the CP test don't appear. With a power meter whose CP hasn't been tested for 42 days the schedule also uses heart rate / pace until one CP test brings power back.
faq.numbers.q: Why do the numbers differ from my watch?
faq.numbers.a: The two sides compute differently and use different thresholds — that is expected; Settings has a side-by-side of the app's and the watch's values.
faq.estimate.a: A number or rule without a direct source in public literature, estimated from your data or common practice and calibrated on your data later.
faq.data.q: Can I take my data with me?
faq.data.a: Yes. Settings downloads all of it (original FIT files included), and you can delete your account.

why.h: Every calculation in the open, every number traceable to a source
why.lead: Many pace calculators do "distance ÷ speed, plus a few minutes per 100 m of climb". This one works out grade, pack, weather and altitude separately, with models from the sports-science literature, then calibrates them on your own records.
why.sources.p: Grade from Minetti's energy cost, pack from Pandolf, CP from Monod, distance from Riegel, heat from the international consensus.
why.sources.ex: Every model's formula and sources; methods and names belong to their authors →
why.zones.p: Daniels, Friel, Seiler, 80/20, Lydiard, Canova, Pfitzinger, Uphill Athlete, Koop… the schedule's intensities mean the same thing these coaches do.
why.calibrated.p: How heat moves your heart rate, how much flat a climb is worth, what counts as all-out, where heart-rate drift is cut, how easy an easy run is… all fitted on what you have run.
why.calibrated.ex: Literature values until there is enough data; the more you log, the more it is you.
why.estimate.l: What isn't certain is marked as such
why.estimate.p: A number without a direct source is always marked "estimate"; a rule the back-test didn't improve says so too.
why.estimate.ex: E.g. the long-race fatigue correction: on {n} trail races its back-test error went from {a}% to {b}%, so it stays marked "estimate".
wf.lead: The example 50K, starting from the flat and adding layer by layer: the climb, the terrain, long-race fatigue, race-day weather and altitude. Each layer is what the calculator adds when it runs again with that factor in; together they make the predicted finish, and each layer names its model.
